newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defectors again choose Hong Kong - reports.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defectors again choose Hong Kong - reports.

text.p: Two more North Koreans, at least one an intelligence agent, have fled to Hong Kong where the biggest defection from the communist nation was announced last week, South Korean media reported on Sunday.
South Korean officials followed their usual practice of not commenting officially on defections in third countries until the escapees were safely in Seoul.

But reports of the latest defection through the British colony of Hong Kong were in all newspapers and on radio and television with the only question being whether both escapees were intelligence agents or only one of them.
Yonhap News Agency quoted a Hong Kong official as saying the colony expected a "rush" of North Korean defectors in the months before it returns to Chinese control in mid-1997.

It said a Hong Kong public security source had identified the latest escapees as Yu Bong-nam, a member of the North Korean Public Security Ministry, and Chon Hak-chol who it described as a North Korean intelligence agent.
However the Korea Broadcasting System said Chon was a North Korean student who had been studying in Beijing, not an intelligence agent.

Yonhap said Yu, who arrived in Hong Kong in October, spied on North Korean students in Beijing while it said Chon was in charge of intelligence work in China against South Korea's own intelligence service, the Agency for National Security Planning. Chon fled to Hong Kong in November.
Yonhap said Yu was recalled to North Korea from Beijing after spying on North Korean students there in 1994. He was demoted and sent to serve as an agent in a rural area.
Unhappy with the demotion, Yu fled back to China and after spending five months there, was smuggled into Hong Kong.
Yonhap said Chon fled to Hong Kong when he believed his life was in danger because of mistakes in his work in China.

The defections were revealed three days after South Korea announced last Thursday that 17 North Koreans -- 16 members of one family and a security guard -- fled through China to Hong Kong in November and were waiting for asylum in South Korea.
It was the biggest mass escape from North Korea since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War.
The previous largest single defection was in 1987 when North Korean doctor Kim Man-chol, his wife and nine other relatives came to the South via Japan.
Diplomatic sources said the 17 were likely to arrive in Seoul this week, possibly as early as Monday.
Yonhap said the latest two escapees brought to 35 the total number of North Koreans who have fled to Hong Kong to seek asylum in South Korea since 1993.

Officials from the Unification Ministry, which deals with inter-Korean matters, said on Friday that South Korea would build its first camp next year to cope with a possible surge in defections from North Korea because of the Stalinist nation's deteriorating economic situation.
The two Koreas are still technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in a truce and not a peace treaty.
A total of 34 North Koreans, excluding the present 19, have so far defected from the Stalinist state to South Korea this year. There were 38 defections last year and 50 in 1994.
Among North Koreans who sought asylum this year were a pilot who flew his MiG-19 across the Korean border and a diplomat at North Korea's Zambian embassy.
